fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk Colorado says female cottonwoods shed their cotton in June, often so heavily that nearby lawns turn white, and that the cotton carries the tree's small seeds on the wind.
quote: Cotton shed by female trees in June is often so abundant that it turns nearby lawns white. … Flowers on female trees, after being pollinated by wind-borne pollen from male trees in April, develop small green capsules that split open in June to shed small seeds carried by wind-borne “cotton”.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1758: Cottonwood Cotton

fact: CSU Extension says cottonwood cotton has no allergenic properties, so allergy symptoms during the June cotton season probably come from grass, weed or tree pollen.
quote: Although cotton can be a nuisance, it has no allergenic properties. People with allergy symptoms during June cotton distribution are probably suffering from other wind-borne pollen – from grasses, weeds or other trees.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1758: Cottonwood Cotton

fact: The Colorado State Forest Service describes plains cottonwood as a tree of floodplains, stream banks, springs and moist woodlands, with leaves 3 to 6 inches long and capsules holding many tiny, cotton-like seeds.
quote: Plains Cottonwood Populus deltoides … Leaves: Broad-leafed foliage is glossy and yellow-green; 3 to 6 inches long, 4 to 6 inches wide; toothed margins. Fruit: Inch long with capsules containing 3 to 4 valves; many tiny, cotton-like seeds inside valves. … Habitat: Found in floodplains, bordering streams, near springs and in moist woodlands; pure stands or with willows.
source_label: Colorado State Forest Service, Colorado's Major Tree Species

fact: The Colorado State Forest Service describes ponderosa pine needles as stiff and 3 to 7 inches long, usually in bundles of three.
quote: Ponderosa Pine Pinus ponderosa … Leaves: Evergreen needles are stiff, dark yellow-green; 3 to 7 inches long; typically in bundles of 3 that form tufts near the ends of branches.
source_label: Colorado State Forest Service, Colorado's Major Tree Species

fact: CSU Extension says evergreens regularly shed their older needles and that Front Range pines, spruces and firs often have a heavy needle drop.
quote: Evergreens normally do shed previous years’ needles on a regular basis. Often there can be a “heavy” needle drop on Front Range landscape pines, spruces and firs.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1760: Excessive Fall Needle Drop

fact: CSU Extension says cottonwoods naturally shed pencil-sized twigs, a process called cladoptosis that is more common in hot, dry summer months.
quote: Fortunately, cladoptosis is a naturally occurring twig drop common to many tree species, including cottonwood. … Take a look at the bottom of the fallen, pencil sized branches underneath the tree. … Cladoptosis is more prevalent during the hot dry summer months.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1768: Small Branch Drop in Cottonwood Trees

fact: CSU Extension says a dry, windy Front Range March and April stresses trees before leaf-out, and that abnormally large seed crops, sometimes tied to a lack of moisture, are a normal response to certain weather.
quote: A dry March and April with frequent high winds stresses trees just before leaf emergence and root growth. … Abnormally large seed crops, sometimes associated with a decline in moisture, are a normal response to certain weather conditions.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1759: Excessive Seed Production on Trees

fact: CSU Extension lists female ash, Siberian elm, honeylocust, hawthorn, crabapple, maple and goldenrain tree among trees that seed themselves in lawns, and says dense grass mowed at 3 inches inhibits most tree seedlings.
quote: Many trees such as female ash, Siberian elm, honeylocust, hawthorn, crabapple, maple and goldenrain tree may seed themselves in lawns. Dense turf and mowing to a 3-inch height should inhibit most tree seedlings.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1538: Control of Tree Seedlings in Lawns

fact: The Colorado Department of Agriculture's noxious weed list puts Siberian elm on List C, the species so widespread and well established across Colorado that statewide eradication is impractical.
quote: List C Species Widely distributed. The species are widespread and well-established throughout the state, making statewide eradication impractical. … Siberian elm Ulmus pumila
source_label: Colorado Department of Agriculture, Colorado Noxious Weed List

fact: The Colorado Department of Agriculture says Siberian elm spreads by seed carried mainly by wind, blooms for about a week in early to mid-spring before its leaves open, and sets its seed in a flat, winged fruit called a samara.
quote: Reproduction is by seed, primarily dispersed by wind, but also by water, animals, and in the undercarriages of equipment and vehicles. … The blooming period occurs from early to mid-spring before the leaves develop, lasting about one week. Seeds develop in a light green, oval-shaped, and flattened wing-like fruit known as a samara.
source_label: Colorado Department of Agriculture, Siberian elm (Ulmus pumila)

fact: The Colorado Department of Agriculture's Siberian elm fact sheet says the seeds can germinate within a week or two in damp conditions and persist in the soil for up to eight years, and that very young seedlings pull fairly easily by hand, especially when the ground is moist.
quote: Under damp conditions, the seeds have the capacity to germinate within a week or two, and can persist in the seed bank for up to eight years. … Very young seedlings can be pulled fairly easily by hand or with a weed-wrench, especially in moist soil conditions.
source_label: Colorado Department of Agriculture, Siberian Elm Identification and Management (List C fact sheet)
notes: Linked from the CDA Siberian elm species page as its fact sheet; hosted on Google Drive.

fact: A 2003 USDA Forest Service analysis of Fort Collins' municipal forest found green ash the most common street tree, at 22% of street trees, with honeylocust at 10.2%.
quote: Green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica) is the most common street tree species, with 3,551 trees accounting for 22% of the population (Table 2). Honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos) accounts for 10.2% all trees.
source_label: USDA Forest Service, Benefit-Cost Analysis of Fort Collins' Municipal Forest (CUFR-2, November 2003)
notes: Street-tree inventory counts only; 2003 data, before emerald ash borer reached Colorado. Table 2 prints 3,552 green ash; the text says 3,551.

fact: USDA's plant fact sheet for honeylocust says thornless, fruitless varieties are used widely in landscaping and along sidewalks, describes its leaves as small and doubly compound, and says the wild tree forms long, twisted seed pods in late summer.
quote: Thornless and fruitless varieties have been developed by the horticultural industry and are used extensively in landscaping. The trees are very hardy and are often used in parking lot islands and along side walks. The open canopy and small leaves will not shade out turf grasses or other landscape plants. … The doubly compound leaves are alternate and dark green in color. … Long, twisted seed pods form in late summer
source_label: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet: Honey Locust (Gleditsia triacanthos)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's maintenance guidelines say leaves and other airborne debris left on synthetic turf migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and compacting the infill, and that organic material should come off quickly to impede algae, weed and moss growth.
quote: Remove airborne contaminants, such as leaves and other debris. If allowed to remain on the surface for any length of time, they will migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and causing infill compaction. … Remove organic material, including animal waste, as soon as possible to impede the growth of algae, weed or moss growth. Leafy trees should not be located next to a field, if possible.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)
notes: Written for infilled sports fields; applied here to infilled yard turf.

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council says light debris can come off with a handheld or backpack blower, and that to keep infill from moving you should not point the nozzle straight into the turf and should use minimal throttle.
quote: Sunflower seeds, peanut shells, pistachio shells, etc. should be removed as soon as possible by using a hand held or back pack blower. To minimize or eliminate the movement of infill, do not point nozzle directly into the turf. Use minimal throttle to decrease the volume of air.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council says surface debris should come off with a mechanical sweeper or other synthetic-turf cleaning equipment, using synthetic bristles and never metal or wire ones.
quote: A mechanical sweeper or other specialty synthetic turf cleaning equipment should be used to remove surface debris. … Use only synthetic fiber bristles of recommended stiffness. Do not use metal or wire bristles.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: In its spill cleanup steps, the Synthetic Turf Council uses a vacuum to take the infill out of the affected area, after which new infill has to be installed.
quote: Vacuum out the infill in the affected area, use a solution of household dishwashing liquid and water to break down and clean any remaining fluid from the turf. Once the turf is clean, you will need to install new infill.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council says every loose foreign object on synthetic turf, however small, can damage it by abrading the fibers or contaminating the infill.
quote: Every loose foreign object, no matter how small, can damage your field by abrading the grass fibers and/or contaminating the infill.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: Motz, an infill maker, says a leaf blower makes quick work of dry leaves but may not suit leaves clumped by a storm or heavy rain, and that holding it about 12 to 18 inches above the turf should avoid moving the infill.
quote: Leaf blowers make a quick task of dried leaves and debris, but they may not be your best option after a big storm or heavy rain when leaves are clumped together and heavier. As long as you keep the leaf blower at a distance of about 12-18 inches above your artificial turf, you should avoid any potential infill migration.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Rake Leaves on Artificial Turf Without Causing Damage (Oct. 6, 2020)

fact: Motz says metal rakes are the tool most likely to damage turf, recommends a lightweight plastic or bamboo rake with curved tines, and says a plain broom can also work.
quote: Heavy metal rakes with metal tines aren’t a good option because they’re the most likely to damage your turf. Instead, look for lightweight plastic or bamboo rakes with curved tines. Some homeowners opt to use a simple broom for this task, which can also work well.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Rake Leaves on Artificial Turf Without Causing Damage (Oct. 6, 2020)

fact: Motz says leaves and twigs can block the holes in turf backing, so debris should come off a few times a year, especially in autumn, with larger sticks picked up before raking.
quote: However, a few times per year, particularly in autumn, you will want to remove debris and fallen leaves. This is because small items, like leaves and twigs, can block the holes in the turf’s backing. … Before you start raking leaves, walk around your lawn and pick up all the larger sticks or debris.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Rake Leaves on Artificial Turf Without Causing Damage (Oct. 6, 2020)

fact: Motz suggests piling raked leaves into garden or landscape beds to break down there.
quote: Alternately, if you have a garden or low-maintenance landscaping beds, pile the leaves into those beds to decompose naturally with time and release beneficial nutrients.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Rake Leaves on Artificial Turf Without Causing Damage (Oct. 6, 2020)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape, a turf maker, calls a leaf blower effective for leaves, pine needles and other light debris but warns that high air pressure can displace or remove infill, so it should run on a low setting at a safe distance with gentle sweeping motions.
quote: Leaf Blower: A leaf blower is an effective tool for clearing leaves, pine needles, and other light debris from your turf surface. However, it should be used with caution, as high air pressure can displace or remove the infill. Opt for a low-power setting, keep the blower at a safe distance from the turf, and use gentle sweeping motions to avoid disturbing the infill.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says pine needles left for long periods get trapped between turf fibers, come off most easily with a low blower or a stiff synthetic broom, and call for a plastic rake, never a metal one, when they build up.
quote: Pine needles can become trapped between turf fibers if left for extended periods. The easiest way to remove them is with a leaf blower on a low setting or a stiff synthetic broom. For stubborn buildup, gently use a plastic rake to lift debris without damaging the turf fibers. Avoid metal rakes, which may damage the backing or grass blades.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says fall leaves should come off regularly, because leaves left over winter can decompose into a layer of organic matter that impedes drainage and encourages moss.
quote: Autumn: As leaves begin to fall, it’s important to remove them regularly. If left to sit over winter, they can decompose and create a layer of organic matter that can impede drainage and encourage moss growth.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says airborne seeds can sprout in the infill or around the edges of turf, and that most such weeds pull easily by hand because their roots are shallow.
quote: Weeds can’t grow through the turf’s backing, but airborne seeds can sometimes sprout in the infill layer or around the edges. Hand-Pulling: The vast majority of weeds can be easily pulled by hand. Their roots are shallow and can’t get a strong grip in the infill.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide

fact: Larimer County Solid Waste's Green Waste Program takes grass and leaves as yard waste, but not bags or weeds, charges loads at the main gate, sends mixed loads to the landfill, and grinds what it takes for use on site.
quote: Green waste must go through the main gate to be charged and tracked. … The following items will be accepted as green waste: … Yard Waste Grass and leaves Garden waste or plant clippings … We will not accept the following as green waste: Bags, containers, fiberboard, food waste, metal, painted wood, plastic, plywood, root balls, soil, trash, treated wood, trunks larger than 2 feet in diameter (these cannot be processed as green waste) and weeds. … All green waste loads must be clean and unloaded by waste type (pallets, green waste, logs, and yard waste). No other trash will be accepted in a load; all mixed loads will go to the landfill. … Green waste is collected, ground up and used on site to add nutrients to soil and prevent erosion.
source_label: Larimer County Solid Waste, Green Waste Program
notes: larimer.gov returns a Cloudflare challenge to curl; the page was read through a fetch tool on 2026-09-25 and matches the independent read in can-you-put-artificial-turf-over-grass-or-dirt.larimer-green-waste-excludes-soil. Fee amounts are on the county landfill fee page and are not quoted here.

fact: CSU Extension says fall leaves are a valuable compost resource, that whole leaves compost better than shredded ones, and that a managed bin can make compost by late spring while an unattended pile may take two to three years.
quote: Fall leaves are a valuable resource because they keep garden soil productive. … Whole leaves are better for compost than leaves that are shredded or mulched with a lawn mower. … By following these simple guidelines, you can produce fall-leaf compost by late spring. An unattended a pile of leaves may take two to three years to decompose.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1612: Composting: Fall Leaves
